through undersigned counsel, and for its Reply Brief states as follows:

                                       INTRODUCTION
       The purpose of a reply brief is to respond to the arguments made by party opponents.

Rather than replying to every argument other parties make in their initial briefs, having

presented and argued its positions in its Initial Post-Hearing Brief, Staff limits its replies to

where further explanation will most aid the Commission in its deliberations. Staff stands on

the arguments made in its Initial Post-Hearing Brief, and silence on any argument or position

should not be taken as acceptance.

                                      LEGAL STANDARD
       In determining each contested issue, the Commission should be ever mindful that

the law places the burden of proof on Evergy Metro, Inc., d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro

(“EMM”). Section 393.150.2, RSMo., provides:

              At any hearing involving a rate sought to be increased, the
              burden of proof to show that the increased rate or proposed
              increased rate is just and reasonable shall be upon the . . .
              electrical corporation . . . and the commission shall give to the
              hearing and decision of such questions preference over all
              other questions pending before it and decide the same as
              speedily as possible.



                                               1
 In its most basic sense, the burden of proof is “that of establishing the affirmative of the

ultimate issue[.]”1 In practical terms, it means that the Company must prove that rates

should be increased. This burden never shifts away from the Company. 2

        As stated on page 9 of Sta ’s Initial Brief, the Commission’s rules likewise state that

when a stipulation and agreement is not unanimous and an objection is ﬁled, the stipulation

shifts procedurally from a settlement to the stipulated position of the signatory parties.

The Commission retains authority to decide the case after hearing. 3

        The Commission has authority under Chapters 386 and 393, RSMo, to regulate

public utility rates and to ensure rates are just and reasonable after considering all relevant

factors.4 The United States Supreme Court in the Hope case established that the rate making

process involves a balancing of the investor and consumer interests. 5 Missouri courts have

upheld that principle in their rulings, balancing the interests of the stakeholders with the

public interest.6

       Other parties in this case have presented a false sense of urgency by suggesting ﬁnal

determinations and ongoing plans must be put in place as a result of this case. Sta

suggests a more tempered and adaptive approach to allow for changes once rates are in

place. In the utility industry there is typically more than one bite at the apple, and the

balancing that may be needed as the industry transitions can always be addressed at a

Stipulations I-IV in their entirety, without modification; and, order Staff’s positions on the

remining issues not covered by Stipulations I-IV.

Issue 1. Cost of Capital
        As argued in pages 21-36 of its Initial Brief, Sta maintains its recommended 52.19%

common equity and 47.81% long-term debt capital structure, 4.54% embedded debt cost,

initial briefs of OPC and EMM.

A. Capital Structure

preserve an equity-rich utility structure while ﬁnancing the consolidated enterprise with

more debt.22 That concern merits examination, but the existence of internal capital

allocation does not establish that a capital structure including 45% equity mirrors EMM’s

appropriate capitalization. In fact, Sta            expressly considered that relationship. Sta

witness, Dr. Seoung Joun Won, PhD found that EMM obtains capital independently, its

securities lack a parent guarantee, the ﬁnancing history did not establish double leverage,

and the parent is not signiﬁcantly diversiﬁed into nonutility operations. 23 Sta also found no

parent long-term debt proceeds used to infuse equity into EMM. 24
